title: How does Flink achieve end-to-end exactly-once semantics (checkpointed state + a two-phase-commit sink via TwoPhaseCommitSinkFunction to Kafka/JDBC/Iceberg: pre-commit on checkpoint, commit on checkpoint-complete)?
shortTitle: How does Flink achieve end-to-end exactly-once
keyPoints: Internal exactly-once is guaranteed by barrier-based checkpointing that snapshots operator state and source offsets consistently.
End-to-end exactly-once extends this to external sinks by tying the sink's transaction lifecycle to the checkpoint lifecycle.
The two-phase commit protocol has four hooks: beginTransaction, preCommit, commit, and abort, mapped to checkpoint events.
The sink pre-commits output when the checkpoint barrier arrives but only commits when the JobManager confirms the checkpoint is globally complete.
Kafka sinks use Kafka transactions so pre-committed records are invisible to read-committed consumers until commit.
The checkpoint interval becomes the end-to-end latency floor for exactly-once output because downstream readers only see data after commit.
If the external system cannot do transactions, you can achieve effectively-once with idempotent writes keyed by a deterministic ID.

s1_definition.oneliner: Flink gets exactly-once end to end by pairing checkpointed state with a sink that pre-commits on checkpoint and only commits when the checkpoint is globally confirmed, so failures roll back uncommitted output.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Internal exactly-once** – Barrier-based checkpointing snapshots all operator state and source offsets so that on recovery, state reflects each record exactly once.
- **End-to-end exactly-once** – Extends internal guarantees to external sinks by tying the sink's transaction to the checkpoint lifecycle.
- **Two-phase commit** – A protocol with four hooks (beginTransaction, preCommit, commit, abort) that ensures the sink only makes output visible when the checkpoint is confirmed complete.
- **Pre-commit** – The sink flushes buffered output into an open transaction and prepares it when the checkpoint barrier arrives, but does not commit.
- **Commit** – Runs only after the JobManager confirms the checkpoint is globally complete, making output visible to downstream consumers.
- **Abort** – Rolls back a transaction that will not be committed, for example on failure before checkpoint completion.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to guarantee that every transaction is written to the external ledger exactly once, never zero times and never twice, even if a server crashes mid-write. The trick is a two-stage signature. When the clerk reaches a checkpoint, they prepare the ledger entries but leave them in a sealed envelope that is not yet filed (pre-commit). Only once head office confirms that the whole checkpoint across all clerks succeeded does the clerk open the envelope and file the entries for real (commit). If a crash happens before head office confirms, the sealed envelope is simply torn up and recovery re-does the work from the last good checkpoint.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  End-to-End Exactly-Once with Two-Phase Commit

  Checkpoint Lifecycle:

  JobManager                 Source        Operator       Sink
      │                        │              │             │
      │──trigger checkpoint──▶│              │             │
      │                        │──barrier──▶ │             │
      │                        │  snapshot   │──barrier──▶│
      │                        │  (offsets)  │  snapshot   │
      │                        │             │  (state)    │ preCommit
      │                        │             │             │ (flush to txn)
      │◀── ack ───────────────│◀── ack ────│◀── ack ────│
      │                                                    │
      │──checkpoint complete──────────────────────────────▶│
      │                                                    │ COMMIT
      │                                                    │ (output visible)


  Failure Before Checkpoint Confirmation:

      │──trigger checkpoint──▶│──barrier──▶│──barrier──▶│
      │                        │            │            │ preCommit
      │                        X  CRASH     │            │
      │                                                  │
      │  Checkpoint NOT confirmed                        │
      │  Sink: ABORT transaction                         │
      │  Recovery: restore last good checkpoint           │
      │  Replay from saved offsets                        │
      │  No duplicate output (transaction was aborted)    │


  Kafka Exactly-Once Visibility:

  Producer (Flink Sink)          Kafka Topic          Consumer
  ─────────────────────          ───────────          ────────
  beginTransaction               │                    │
  write R1, R2, R3              │ R1,R2,R3 (uncommit) │
  preCommit                      │                    │ (invisible)
  ... checkpoint confirmed ...   │                    │
  COMMIT                         │ R1,R2,R3 (committed)│
                                 │                    │ NOW VISIBLE
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
End-to-end exactly-once in Flink means every input record affects the final external output exactly once, even across failures. It is achieved by combining two mechanisms. The first is barrier-based checkpointing, which gives exactly-once state consistency internally: barriers flow through the graph, operators snapshot a consistent cut, and on recovery Flink restores state and rewinds sources. The second is the two-phase commit protocol for the sink, which ties the external transaction to the checkpoint lifecycle.

The protocol has four hooks. beginTransaction opens a new external transaction when a checkpoint interval starts. preCommit runs when the checkpoint barrier reaches the sink: it flushes buffered output into the transaction and prepares it, but does not commit. commit runs only after the JobManager confirms the checkpoint is globally complete, making output visible. abort rolls back a transaction on failure. Because the commit happens only on checkpoint completion, any failure before that leaves the transaction uncommitted.

At the National Bank of India we used this for our settlement ledger pipeline. The Kafka sink used Kafka transactions with a transactional ID prefix, and the accounting consumers read in read-committed mode so they only saw settlements after the commit. When I simulated a crash after pre-commit but before confirmation, the sink aborted the uncommitted transaction, recovery replayed the same settlements, and they ended up committed exactly once with no duplicates.

The key senior points are that the checkpoint interval becomes the latency floor for exactly-once output, that the Kafka transaction timeout must exceed your checkpoint interval plus recovery time, and that if the sink cannot do transactions you can fall back to idempotent writes.

Remember one sentence: End-to-end exactly-once pairs checkpointed state with a two-phase-commit sink that pre-commits on barrier and commits only when the checkpoint is globally confirmed.
